claim: Protein mobility in the cytoplasm depends on protein surface properties and ionic strength.
source: We studied the dependence of protein mobility on protein surface properties and ionic strength.
evidence: This is the main research question stated in the abstract, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: In E. coli, the translational diffusion coefficient (D) depends on the net charge and its distribution over the protein.
source: We find that in E. coli D depends on the net charge and its distribution over the protein, with positive proteins diffusing up to 100-fold slower than negative ones.
evidence: Supported by FRAP measurements shown in Figures 1 and 3, demonstrating the relationship between charge and diffusion.

claim: Positive proteins diffuse up to 100-fold slower than negative ones in E. coli.
source: We find that in E. coli D depends on the net charge and its distribution over the protein, with positive proteins diffusing up to 100-fold slower than negative ones.
evidence: Quantified from FRAP data comparing -30 GFP (10-11 µm²/s) to +25 GFP (0.14 µm²/s) in Figure 1d.

claim: The effect of charge on protein diffusion is weaker in L. lactis and Hfx. volcanii due to electrostatic screening.
source: This effect is weaker in L. lactis and Hfx. volcanii due to electrostatic screening.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparative FRAP measurements across three organisms shown in Figure 2, correlated with their different ionic strengths.

claim: The decrease in mobility of positive proteins is caused by interaction with ribosomes.
source: The decrease in mobility is probably caused by interaction of positive FPs with ribosomes as shown in in vivo diffusion measurements and confirmed in vitro with purified ribosomes.
evidence: Supported by rifampicin experiments (Figure 4b), sucrose gradient co-localization (Figure 5a-c), and in vitro binding assays (Figure 5d-g).

claim: Ribosome surface properties may limit the composition of the cytoplasmic proteome.
source: Ribosome surface properties may thus limit the composition of the cytoplasmic proteome.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that positive proteins bind to ribosomes and diffuse slowly, combined with proteome analysis showing predominantly negative proteins (Figure 7).

claim: E. coli has a cytoplasmic K+ concentration of 0.2 M.
source: These three organisms differ in their cytoplasmic ionic strength as shown by measurements on the dominant cation, K+: E. coli (0.2 M) (Shabala et al., 2009)
evidence: Cited from literature reference Shabala et al., 2009.

claim: L. lactis has a cytoplasmic K+ concentration of 0.8 M.
source: L. lactis (0.8 M) (Poolman et al., 1987)
evidence: Cited from literature reference Poolman et al., 1987.

claim: Hfx. volcanii has a cytoplasmic K+ concentration of 2.1 M.
source: Hfx. volcanii (2.1 M) (Pérez-Fillol and Rodríguez-Valera, 1986)
evidence: Cited from literature reference Pérez-Fillol and Rodríguez-Valera, 1986.

claim: The -30, -7, and 0 variants of GFP all have the same mean diffusion coefficient of 10-11 µm²/s in E. coli.
source: The −30, –7 and 0 variants of GFP all have the same mean diffusion coefficient of 10–11 µm2/s (for table of mean diffusion coefficients see Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Directly measured by FRAP and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The mean diffusion coefficient of +25 GFP in E. coli is 0.14 µm²/s.
source: down to a mean value of 0.14 µm2/s for +25 GFP.
evidence: Directly measured by FRAP and shown in Figure 1d and Supplementary file 1B.

claim: For +25 GFP to diffuse with a coefficient as low as 0.14 µm²/s, it needs to bind to membrane proteins, DNA, and/or ribosome-mRNA complexes.
source: Based on a census of elements present in E. coli cells this means that for +25 GFP to diffuse with a diffusion coefficient as low as 0.14 µm2/s it needs to bind to membrane proteins, DNA and/or ribosome-mRNA complexes.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of +25 GFP diffusion coefficient with known diffusion coefficients of cellular components.

claim: Membrane proteins with 12-14 transmembrane helices in E. coli and L. lactis have D = 0.02-0.03 µm²/s.
source: For membrane proteins with 12–14 transmembrane helices in E. coli and L. lactis, D is 0.02–0.03 µm2/s (Mika et al., 2014; Kumar et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from literature references Mika et al., 2014 and Kumar et al., 2010.

claim: DNA in E. coli has apparent diffusion coefficient values of 0.000035-0.00007 µm²/s.
source: Describing the motion of DNA with a diffusion coefficient is somewhat of a stretch, as its parts do not move freely, but apparent values of 0.000035–0.00007 µm2/s have been reported (Reyes-Lamothe et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from literature reference Reyes-Lamothe et al., 2008.

claim: Ribosome-mRNA complexes in E. coli have a diffusion coefficient of 0.04 µm²/s when a one-component model is used.
source: In fast growing cells, we expect ribosomes and mRNA to be associated most of the time (Sanamrad et al., 2014), and D is 0.04 µm2/s when a one-component model is used for fitting the data (Bakshi et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from literature references Sanamrad et al., 2014 and Bakshi et al., 2012.

claim: Free ribosomes have D = 0.40 µm²/s (~15%) and bound ribosomes have D = 0.055 µm²/s (~85%).
source: In another study free and bound ribosomes were discriminated and D values of 0.40 (~15%) and 0.055 µm2/s (~85%) were found (Sanamrad et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from literature reference Sanamrad et al., 2014.

claim: The mean diffusion coefficient of -7 GFP in L. lactis (6.2 µm²/s) is lower than in E. coli (10 µm²/s).
source: For L. lactis the mean diffusion coefficient of −7 GFP (6.2 µm2/s) is lower than for E. coli (10 µm2/s).
evidence: Directly measured by FRAP and shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1B.

claim: The mean diffusion coefficient of +25 GFP is higher in L. lactis (0.61 µm²/s) than in E. coli (0.14 µm²/s).
source: However, D drops less with positive net charge so that for +25 GFP the mean diffusion coefficient is higher in L. lactis (0.61 µm2/s) than in E. coli (0.14 µm2/s).
evidence: Directly measured by FRAP and shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1B.

claim: The higher cytoplasmic ionic strength of L. lactis reduces the affinity of positive GFPs to negatively-charged binding partners.
source: This can be explained by the higher cytoplasmic ionic strength of L. lactis, reducing the affinity of positive GFPs to hypothetical negatively-charged binding partners.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of diffusion data across organisms with different ionic strengths.

claim: In Hfx. volcanii, the mean diffusion coefficient drops from 5.5 µm²/s for -7 GFP to 1.9 µm²/s for +25 GFP.
source: For Hfx. volcanii the drop in diffusion coefficient is even less steep, with the mean diffusion coefficient dropping from 5.5 µm2/s, for −7 GFP, to 1.9 µm2/s, for +25 GFP.
evidence: Directly measured by FRAP and shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1B.

claim: In Hfx. volcanii, the diffusion coefficient of -30 GFP (10 µm²/s) is higher than that of -7 GFP (5.5 µm²/s).
source: We also note that in Hfx. volcanii the diffusion coefficient of −30 GFP is higher than of −7 GFP, 10 µm2/s compared to 5.5 µm2/s, which may be caused by a less negative binding partner for GFP in Hfx. volcanii than in E. coli.
evidence: Directly measured by FRAP and shown in Figure 2.

claim: After osmotic upshift to 1.2 Osm, the diffusion coefficients of all GFP variants in E. coli dropped.
source: In 1.2 Osm medium the diffusion coefficients of all variants dropped (Figure 3a and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Directly measured by FRAP after osmotic upshift, shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The fold-change in diffusion coefficient after osmotic upshift to 1.2 Osm is 56-fold for -30 GFP, 28-fold for -7 GFP, 16-fold for +15 GFP, and 7-fold for +25 GFP.
source: The degree of the drop is 56-, 28-, 16-, and 7-fold (between medians) for −30, –7, +15 and +25, respectively
evidence: Calculated from FRAP measurements before and after osmotic upshift, shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The fold-change in diffusion is less for positive proteins because electrostatic screening may partly compensate for the increased crowding effect.
source: Thus, the fold-change is less for the positive proteins because the electrostatic screening may compensate partly for the increased crowding effect.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that positive proteins show smaller fold-changes in diffusion after osmotic upshift.

claim: The mean diffusion coefficient of +11b GFP is 2.7 µm²/s and that of +11a GFP is 0.76 µm²/s in E. coli.
source: The mean diffusion coefficient of +11b GFP is 2.7 µm2/s and that of +11a GFP is 0.76 µm2/s (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Directly measured by FRAP, shown in Figure 3c and Supplementary file 1B.

claim: The distribution of charge over the GFP surface affects the diffusion coefficient.
source: So, it clearly matters how the net charge is distributed over the GFP surface.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing +11a and +11b GFP variants with the same net charge but different charge distributions, shown in Figure 3c-d.

claim: +25 GFP does not co-localize with DNA in E. coli.
source: In nine cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–i) out of 46 the nucleoid had shrunk and in all these cells + 25 GFP did not co-localize with DNA.
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy with DRAQ-5 DNA staining and chloramphenicol treatment, shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: DNA is not the major binding partner for +25 GFP.
source: We conclude that DNA is not the major binding partner for +25 GFP.
evidence: Based on co-localization experiments showing +25 GFP does not follow DNA distribution.

claim: The drop in +25 GFP diffusion rate is not dependent on DNA.
source: This shows that the drop in +25 GFP diffusion rate is not dependent on DNA.
evidence: Demonstrated by FRAP measurements in DNA-free regions showing similar differences between -7 and +25 GFP, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: After treatment with rifampicin, the diffusion coefficient of +25 GFP increases for 20 min and then levels off.
source: We found that after treatment with rifampicin, the diffusion coefficient of +25 GFP increases for 20 min and then levels off.
evidence: Directly measured by time-course FRAP after rifampicin addition, shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of +25 GFP after 20 min of rifampicin treatment is close to the value of the 30S ribosomal subunit.
source: Importantly, the diffusion coefficient after 20 min of rifampicin treatment is close to the value of the 30S and presumably the 50S subunit.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4b where +25 GFP diffusion coefficient approaches the dashed line indicating 30S ribosome diffusion.

claim: The positive GFP variants bind to ribosomes, and this is the major cause for their slow diffusion.
source: Together, these findings indicate that the positive GFP variants bind to ribosomes, and that this is the major cause for their slow diffusion.
evidence: Concluded from rifampicin experiments, co-localization studies, and in vitro binding assays.

claim: +25 GFP co-localizes with ribosomes on sucrose gradients.
source: We observed a clear difference in the position of −7 and +25 GFP along the gradient, with the peak of the +25 GFP distribution coinciding with the presence of ribosomes (Figure 5a and c).
evidence: Demonstrated by sucrose gradient centrifugation with fluorescence detection and electron microscopy, shown in Figure 5a and c.

claim: Even at the highest concentration of DNA tested, +25 GFP co-localizes with ribosomes and not with DNA on sucrose gradients.
source: Even at the highest concentration of DNA, +25 GFP co-localizes with ribosomes and not with DNA (Figure 5b).
evidence: Demonstrated by sucrose gradient experiments with added purified DNA, shown in Figure 5b.

claim: +25 GFP binds predominantly to ribosomes.
source: From the combination of sucrose gradient experiments and our in vivo studies described above, we conclude that +25 GFP binds predominantly to ribosomes.
evidence: Concluded from multiple lines of evidence including sucrose gradients, rifampicin experiments, and DNA-free region studies.

claim: Purified +25 GFP associates and aggregates with purified ribosomes at physiological salt concentrations.
source: At physiological salt concentrations (Shabala et al., 2009) we observe that upon mixing ribosomes and +25 GFP, aggregates are formed (Figure 5e).
evidence: Demonstrated by size-exclusion chromatography and fluorescence imaging of purified components, shown in Figure 5d-f.

claim: -7 GFP does not bind to ribosomes.
source: The control experiment with −7 GFP shows that the anionic protein does not bind to ribosomes and elutes on SEC at around 17.5 ml (Figure 5g).
evidence: Demonstrated by size-exclusion chromatography showing no change in elution profile when -7 GFP is mixed with ribosomes, shown in Figure 5g.

claim: In E. coli under the growth conditions used, the number of ribosomes per µm³ is about 17000, corresponding to a concentration of 10 µM.
source: For E. coli, under our growth conditions, the number of ribosomes per µm3 is about 17000 (Vendeville et al., 2011), which corresponds to a concentration of 10 µM.
evidence: Cited from literature reference Vendeville et al., 2011 and converted to concentration.

claim: The ribosome has a diameter of 20 nm and a surface area of 1260 nm², with about half being RNA (630 nm²).
source: The ribosome has a diameter of 20 nm, which yields a surface area of 1260 nm2, assuming a spherical shape. About half of this surface area is RNA so we end up with 630 nm2.
evidence: Calculated from known ribosome dimensions using geometric assumptions.

claim: The maximal number of GFP binding sites on a ribosome is 66.
source: The diameter of GFP is 3.5 nm, giving a 9.6 nm2 cross section. Dividing the ribosome RNA surface area by the GFP cross section gives a maximal number of binding sites of 66.
evidence: Calculated from geometric considerations of ribosome RNA surface area and GFP cross-sectional area.

claim: The Kd for binding of +25 GFP to a ribosome binding site is 6.7 µM in E. coli.
source: Using a fraction of bound +25 GFP of 0.99 in E. coli, we obtain Kd = 6.7 µM.
evidence: Calculated from the fraction of bound GFP and the concentration of binding sites using equilibrium binding equations.

claim: The Kd for binding of +25 GFP to a ribosome binding site is 65 µM for L. lactis and 155 µM for Hfx. volcanii.
source: If we make the assumption that the concentration of ribosomes in L. lactis and Hfx. volcanii is the same as in E. coli, then the Kd for binding of +25 GFP to a ribosome binding site is 65 µM for L. lactis and 155 µM for Hfx. volcanii.
evidence: Calculated from diffusion data assuming similar ribosome concentrations across organisms.

claim: The binding of +25 GFP to ribosomes can be described by electrostatic interactions and screening by small ions on top of a base non-ionic interaction component.
source: Together the results for the relation between Kd and ionic strength, and Deff and GFP charge, show that the binding of GFP to ribosomes can be described by electrostatic interactions and screening by small ions on top of a base non-ionic interaction component.
evidence: Demonstrated by fitting the data with Debye-Hückel-based equations (Equations 3-5) shown in Figure 6.

claim: In all three organisms (E. coli, L. lactis, Hfx. volcanii), the majority of cytoplasmic proteins is acidic and thus negatively charged at physiological internal pH of 7.5.
source: From the pI distributions it is clear that in all three organisms the majority of cytoplasmic proteins is acidic and thus negatively charged at the physiological internal pH of 7.5
evidence: Demonstrated by proteome analysis shown in Figure 7a.

claim: In E. coli, 35 cytoplasmic proteins have a net charge higher than +10, consisting of 18 ribosomal, 9 RNA-associated, 5 DNA-associated and 3 uncharacterized proteins.
source: In E. coli 35 cytoplasmic proteins have a net charge higher than +10. These consist of 18 ribosomal, 9 RNA-associated, 5 DNA-associated and 3 uncharacterized proteins.
evidence: Determined by computational proteome analysis.

claim: All three organisms (E. coli, L. lactis, Hfx. volcanii) essentially have no 'free' positive cytoplasmic proteins.
source: Thus, all three organisms essentially have no 'free' positive cytoplasmic proteins.
evidence: Concluded from proteome analysis showing that highly positive proteins are associated with ribosomes, RNA, or DNA.

claim: The drop in diffusion coefficient with increased positive charge may partly explain why the proteome is mostly negative in E. coli, L. lactis and Hfx. volcanii.
source: The drop in diffusion coefficient with increased positive charge may partly explain why the proteome is mostly negative in E. coli, L. lactis and Hfx. volcanii.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of diffusion data and proteome analysis.

claim: Positive proteins not only diffuse slowly but their binding to ribosomes might also inhibit protein synthesis by affecting the assembly or activity of ribosomes.
source: Positive proteins not only diffuse slowly but their binding to ribosomes might also inhibit protein synthesis, that is, by affecting the assembly or the activity of ribosomes.
evidence: Speculated based on the observed binding of positive proteins to ribosomes.

claim: Ribosomal proteins RplT and RplB in E. coli have net charges of +24 and +31, respectively.
source: The most extreme cases, RplT and RplB, with net charges of +24 and +31, would have a drop in diffusion coefficient of 100-fold.
evidence: Determined from proteome analysis.

claim: The synthesis of cationic ribosomal proteins and the assembly of ribosomes should be highly coordinated and preferably be modular to minimize unwanted side-effects of nonspecific interactions.
source: An implication of our findings is that the synthesis of cationic ribosomal proteins and the assembly of ribosomes should be highly coordinated and preferably be modular to minimize unwanted side-effects of nonspecific interactions (Davis et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from the finding that positive ribosomal proteins would bind nonspecifically to assembled ribosomes, with citation to Davis et al., 2016.

claim: Buchnera aphidicola, Blochmannia floridanus, Onion yellows phytoplasma, and Wigglesworthia glossinidia brevipalpis are (endo)symbionts with small genomes of 572-730 protein-encoding genes.
source: A conundrum is encountered when we look at the proteomes of the bacteria Buchnera aphidicola, Blochmannia floridanus, Onion yellows phytoplasma, and Wigglesworthia glossinidia brevipalpis. All four organisms are (endo)symbionts of plants or insects and have small genomes: 572–730 protein-encoding genes.
evidence: Determined from proteome database analysis.

claim: The four symbiotic bacteria (Buchnera aphidicola, Blochmannia floridanus, Onion yellows phytoplasma, Wigglesworthia glossinidia brevipalpis) have very basic proteomes.
source: All of these have very basic proteomes (Figure 7b and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by proteome analysis shown in Figure 7b and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: It is unclear how symbiotic bacteria with basic proteomes are able to deal with, or avoid, slow diffusion and ribosomes getting swarmed with positive proteins.
source: It is unclear how these organisms are able to deal with, or avoid, slow diffusion and ribosomes getting swarmed with positive proteins.
evidence: This is a paradox identified by the authors based on their findings and proteome analysis.

claim: A protein can diffuse only as slow as the combination of this protein and the slowest component it binds to in the cell.
source: A protein can diffuse only as slow as the combination of this protein and the slowest component it binds to in the cell.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle described by Equation (1) and illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of GFP is faster in the cytoplasm of osmotically-adapted E. coli cells than in osmotically-upshifted cells, even at similar cytoplasmic macromolecule volume fraction.
source: Second, the diffusion coefficient of GFP is faster in the cytoplasm of osmotically-adapted E. coli cells than in osmotically-upshifted cells, even at similar cytoplasmic macromolecule volume fraction (Konopka et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from literature reference Konopka et al., 2009.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of GFP drops much faster with cell volume (after an osmotic upshift) in Lactococcus lactis than in E. coli.
source: Third, the diffusion coefficient of GFP drops much faster with cell volume (after an osmotic upshift) in Lactococcus lactis than in E. coli (Mika et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from literature reference Mika et al., 2014.

claim: The slowing of diffusion in metabolic energy-depleted cells suggests changes in the dynamic structure of the cytoplasm.
source: Fourth, the slowing of diffusion in metabolic energy-depleted cells suggests changes in the dynamic structure of the cytoplasm (Parry et al., 2014; Joyner et al., 2016; Munder et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from literature references Parry et al., 2014; Joyner et al., 2016; Munder et al., 2016.

claim: Binding of tRNA complexes to the ribosome is a diffusion-limited process that leads to limitation in cell growth.
source: Examples of diffusion-limited processes are binding of tRNA complexes to the ribosome, which leads to limitation in cell growth (Klumpp et al., 2013)
evidence: Cited from literature reference Klumpp et al., 2013.

claim: The binding of barstar to barnase is diffusion limited because the proteins are designed to have an increased association rate by electrostatic interactions.
source: and the binding of barstar to barnase, which we know to be diffusion limited because the proteins are designed to have an increased association rate by electrostatic interactions (Vijayakumar et al., 1998).
evidence: Cited from literature reference Vijayakumar et al., 1998.

claim: Only 50 protein types make up 85% of the cytoplasmic proteome of E. coli.
source: though only 50 protein types make up 85% of the cytoplasmic proteome of E. coli (McGuffee et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from literature reference McGuffee et al., 2010.

claim: NMR studies reveal that there are weak interactions between E. coli proteins and proteins cytochrome c, ubiquitin, and calmodulin.
source: NMR studies on proteins, either in the E. coli cytoplasm (Crowley et al., 2011; Ye et al., 2013) or cell lysates (Latham and Kay, 2013), reveal that there are weak interactions between E. coli proteins and proteins cytochrome c, ubiquitin, and calmodulin.
evidence: Cited from literature references Crowley et al., 2011; Ye et al., 2013; Latham and Kay, 2013.

claim: In E. coli, more highly expressed proteins are constrained in evolution to be less sticky.
source: In a computational study on protein interactions it was found that in E. coli more highly expressed proteins are constrained in evolution to be less sticky (Levy et al., 2012), suggesting that nonspecific interactions are common and consequential.
evidence: Cited from literature reference Levy et al., 2012.

claim: The 30S ribosomal subunit in E. coli increases its diffusion coefficient from 0.04 µm²/s to 0.6 µm²/s after treatment with rifampicin.
source: It has been shown that the 30S ribosomal subunit in E. coli increases its diffusion coefficient, from 0.04 µm2/s to 0.6 µm2/s, after treatment with rifampicin (Bakshi et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from literature reference Bakshi et al., 2012.

claim: After adding rifampicin to E. coli cells, the pool of mRNA plummets, with 90% of the mRNAs having a half time of less than 8 min.
source: Rifampicin stops transcription and after adding it to E. coli cells the pool of mRNA plummets, with 90% of the mRNAs having a half time of less than 8 min (Bernstein et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from literature reference Bernstein et al., 2002.

claim: The fluorescence of +25 GFP expressing cells becomes more homogenous after rifampicin treatment.
source: We also find that the fluorescence of +25 GFP expressing cells becomes more homogenous after rifampicin treatment.
evidence: Observed during rifampicin time-course experiments.

claim: The variation in diffusion coefficient between cells is smaller in the presence than in the absence of rifampicin.
source: Finally, we find that the variation in diffusion coefficient between cells is smaller in the presence than in the absence of rifampicin, suggesting that part of the spread in the diffusion relates to ongoing transcription.
evidence: Observed in rifampicin experiments shown in Figure 4b.

claim: In E. coli, there is a big difference (35-fold) between the mean diffusion coefficient of -7 and +25 GFP in DNA-free regions after treatment with cephalexin and chloramphenicol.
source: There is a big difference between the mean diffusion coefficient of −7 and +25 GFP after treatment and in the absence of DNA (35-fold).
evidence: Measured by FRAP in DNA-free regions, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2c.

claim: A similar difference (85-fold) between -7 and +25 GFP was found in cells that were not treated and in the presence of DNA.
source: A similar difference between −7 and +25 GFP was found in cells that were not treated and in the presence of DNA (85-fold).
evidence: Calculated from FRAP data in untreated cells.

claim: +25 GFP is somewhat excluded from DNA (nucleoid), with the effect being largest for +25 GFP compared to -7 GFP.
source: Both −7 and +25 GFP are somewhat excluded from DNA (nucleoid) but the effect is largest for +25 GFP; this is another piece of evidence suggesting that +25 GFP binds to ribosome-mRNA and not to DNA.
evidence: Observed in fluorescence images and co-localization experiments.

claim: In Hfx. volcanii, even with its high internal ion concentration, a major fraction (0.81) of +25 GFP is still bound to ribosomes.
source: From the analysis we conclude that even in Hfx. volcanii, with its high internal ion concentration, a major fraction (0.81) of +25 GFP is still bound to ribosomes.
evidence: Calculated using Equation (1) from diffusion data, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: GFP probably binds to the RNA that is exposed on the surface of the ribosome and probably does so nonspecifically.
source: GFP probably binds to the RNA that is exposed on the surface of the ribosome and probably does so nonspecifically.
evidence: Inferred from the electrostatic nature of the interaction and the negatively charged RNA surface.

claim: The concentration of ribosome binding sites in E. coli is 660 µM.
source: This means that the concentration of binding sites is 660 µM.
evidence: Calculated from ribosome concentration (10 µM) and number of binding sites per ribosome (66).

claim: The fraction of bound +25 GFP in E. coli is 0.99.
source: Using a fraction of bound +25 GFP of 0.99 in E. coli, we obtain Kd = 6.7 µM.
evidence: Calculated from diffusion data using Equation (1).

claim: The ionic strength dependence of the interaction of +25 GFP with ribosomes is similar to that of barnase-barstar, colicinE9-Im9, and thrombin-hirudin protein pairs.
source: The ionic strength dependence of the interaction of +25 GFP with ribosomes (recorded in E. coli, L. lactis and Hfx. volcanii; Figure 6b) is similar to that of the three protein pairs in dilute solutions (Figure 6a); the Kd increases with ionic strength and levels off at higher ionic strength.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing the data in Figure 6a and 6b.

claim: A non-ionic interaction component is needed for proper fitting of the +25 GFP-ribosome binding data.
source: We had expected that the non-ionic interaction free energy would be close to zero, but if we impose this conditions the fit becomes bad (Figure 6c).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing fits with and without non-ionic component in Figure 6b and 6c.

claim: When using a log scale to represent the diffusion coefficient, there is a linear dependence of diffusion coefficient with net charge from 0 to +25 in E. coli.
source: When we use a log scale to represent the diffusion coefficient we see a linear dependence of diffusion coefficient with net charge from 0 to +25 (for E. coli).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6d where the data points follow a linear trend on a log scale.
